query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a high-throughput combinatorial synthesis approach via co-sputtering to fabricate composition-spread thin films of HfNbTaTiZr will reveal that deliberate, systematic variations in individual elemental percentages lead to measurable and localized differences in mechanical properties compared to equiatomic compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in an equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) thin film form serving as the baseline state.
generation.intervention: Employ co-sputtering to create thin films that exhibit a continuous compositional gradient where the percentage of each element is varied away from the equiatomic ratio.
generation.conditions: Standard laboratory conditions at ambient temperature using localized mechanical testing techniques (such as nanoindentation and micro-compression), along with compositional (EDS) and microstructural (TEM/XRD) characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of local microstructural variations including differences in lattice distortion, grain size, and possible minor phase changes induced by non-equiatomic compositions.
generation.mechanism: Systematic alterations in elemental percentages modify the local lattice structure and distortion, thereby affecting dislocation mobility and the balance of strengthening mechanisms, which leads to changes in local hardness and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Regions enriched in elements with larger atomic radii (e.g., increased Hf content) are expected to exhibit increased hardness; other compositional variations may either enhance or reduce yield strength relative to the equiatomic baseline, with these trends being clearly resolved across the compositional gradient.
generation.baseline: Measurements from regions of the thin film that retain the equiatomic composition under identical testing conditions serve as the control baseline.
generation.boundary: The observed effects are specific to the thin film scale under ambient laboratory conditions; extrapolation to bulk materials or extreme environments remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While a directional trend is expected, the magnitude and interplay of multiple compositional effects may introduce complexities that are not fully predictable, necessitating careful interpretation of property variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HfNbTaTiZr thin films using co-sputtering to create continuous compositional gradients. Conduct localized mechanical testing (nanoindentation for hardness and micro-compression for yield strength) at regular compositional intervals. Use EDS mapping to accurately correlate local composition with mechanical properties and perform microstructural characterization (using TEM/XRD) to confirm structural variations. Compare these results to a control sample with equiatomic composition.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via TEM or XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the localized mechanical properties do not vary systematically with the compositional changes—i.e., if regions with altered individual element percentages exhibit mechanical responses statistically equivalent to the equiatomic baseline, or if microstructural variations expected from compositional shifts are absent—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloys mostly focused on overall mechanical performance using equiatomic (or near‐equiatomic) systems processed by casting, powder metallurgy, or additive manufacturing. Several studies have fine‐tuned processing conditions or introduced small dopants (e.g., Hf or Mo) to modify secondary phases or improve mechanical strength without systematically varying the individual elemental compositions. Moreover, work on HfNbTaTiZr in equiatomic form and computational studies on SRO have hinted at compositional influence, but none have specifically targeted the isolated impact of each element.
decision.unsolved: There remains a gap in methodically disentangling the contribution of individual elements on mechanical properties by deliberately moving away from equiatomic compositions. In other words, a systematic, controlled variation in element percentages with direct, localized property evaluation is not yet established.
decision.lever: high-throughput combinatorial synthesis via techniques such as co-sputtering to create composition-spread thin films coupled with localized mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation or micro-compression)
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the need to systematically vary the percentage of each constituent while establishing direct correlations between compositional gradients and mechanical performance. It follows naturally from prior studies that kept composition fixed and now motivates the use of new measurement techniques that can resolve individual elemental effects.
